name: Rania Haddad
headline: 28, part-time university tutor and freelance translator, Amman
description:
Rania Haddad arrives at the university before the heat sets in, her worn leather satchel creaking under the weight of marked essays and a dish towel knotted around leftover bread and a small jar of apricot jam. She teaches three sections of academic writing on a per-course contract, which means no office, no health insurance, and a paycheck that evaporates by mid-month. She never mentions this to her students. Instead, she spreads the bread and jam on her desk during office hours, cutting slices with a plastic knife she keeps in her bag. When a student lingers after questions, she gestures to the chair beside her and waits, her head tilted, the way she does when a draft needs untangling.

At home, in the two-bedroom apartment she shares with her younger brother, his wife, and their toddler, she has turned the kitchen table into a classroom. Three evenings a week, after dinner is cleared, students who cannot afford internet arrive with notebooks and borrowed textbooks. Rania writes on the back of used envelopes, saves every scrap of paper, and explains thesis statements with the same patience she once used to coax her grandmother through Arabic poetry. Her brother teases her about the electricity bill, but he always makes tea. His wife washes the teacups without complaint.

Rania's own marriage ended two years ago, quietly, without a formal announcement. Her ex-husband's family had expected her to stop teaching after the wedding. She did not. When it became clear that her independence was a threat to his authority, they separated. She returned to Amman with two suitcases, a few books, and a determination to never again surrender the work that made her feel real. She moved in with her brother as a temporary arrangement that has stretched into a permanent one. She contributes what she can from her freelance Arabic-to-English translations, but the income is unpredictable. She translates legal documents at night, her fingers tapping until the small hours, the blue glow of her laptop the only light in the living room.

She is warm, but not indiscriminately. She remembers every student who once mentioned a sick mother or a broken printer. She carries a mental roster of who needs a quiet word and who needs a copy of her lecture notes. She does not lecture them about effort or responsibility; she simply shows up with bread and answers. What she struggles with is accepting help. When her sister-in-law buys her a new scarf, Rania insists on folding it into the communal laundry. She keeps a small ledger of her debts, even the ones in kindness.

Rania believes in education as a door, but also as a discipline. She can be impatient with sloppy thinking, yet she never turns away a student who wants to talk. She knows what it is to have your words ignored, so she listens, fully, even when the hallway is emptying and her bus ticket home is already in her pocket.
